memory_line: COPD: aim for 88 to 92. Never zero.
caption_lesson:
🌙 Night shift, 2:15 AM. He's 72 with COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), admitted with pneumonia.
• SpO2 (oxygen saturation) 82%, breathing 28, using his neck muscles

❌ 3 mistakes, 3 error types
1️⃣ Beyond the stem: "His normal's probably low." No baseline was charted
2️⃣ Habit over standard: held the oxygen for "COPD drive"
3️⃣ Acted too late: called drowsy "sleeping", no recheck
➡️ 3:20 AM: SpO2 74%, hard to wake. Rapid response.

🫁 Oxygen in COPD (88 TO 92, NEVER ZERO)
• Low oxygen kills faster than high CO2 (carbon dioxide)
• Some COPD patients hold on to CO2, so too much oxygen can also make them drowsy
• The answer is controlled oxygen, not none

✅ The right move
• Low oxygen? Give oxygen. Never withhold it
• COPD with a CO2 risk: aim for SpO2 88 to 92%, as ordered
• Nasal cannula or a Venturi mask, as ordered or per protocol
• Recheck SpO2, breathing and alertness. Drowsy or confused? Call now, blood gas as ordered

🧠 COPD: aim for 88 to 92. Never zero.

rn_checks: Target SpO2 88 to 92% for patients at risk of hypercapnic (CO2) respiratory failure, such as COPD (BTS 2017). Vera did not check the exact wording inside the GOLD 2027 report
Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic patient; controlled oxygen via nasal cannula or Venturi 24 to 28%, as ordered or per protocol
Drowsiness can be hypoxia OR rising CO2: call, ABG (arterial blood gas) as ordered
